Meta-Harness - Automated model harness optimization, explained clearly
This article covers the latest research paper coming out of Stanford. Meta-Harness is a system designed to automate the engineering of the "harnesses" that surround large language models (LLMs).
Yoonho Lee
@yoonholeee
·
Mar 30
How can we autonomously improve LLM harnesses on problems humans are actively working on? Doing so requires solving a hard, long-horizon credit-assignment problem over all prior code, traces, and scores. Announcing Meta-Harness: a method for optimizing harnesses end-to-end
Yoonho Lee and 5 others
Let's go!

First of all what is a harness?

Everything in your AI system that is not the LLM itself is a harness.
Example: Claude Opus 4.6 is the LLM. Claude Code is the harness.
The harness sits around the LLM as a scaffold and manages how the context is delivered to it, and actually executes the actions the LLM wants to take.
While designing harnesses, we are usually balancing a bunch of important stakeholders. If you considered this whole thing a game, then the optimal harness is a game theory optimization problem. Every actor has it's own goal and motivation, and the Nash equilibrium is when everybody wins. Let's see what the actors are and what they want:
  1. The User wants the AI to do the job fully, correctly, fast, and not get rate-limited.
  2. The Provider wants the user to pay them money, buy their subscription, and deliver value at minimal cost. Lower output tokens, lower tool calls, maximize KV cache, good compaction, etc.
  3. The LLM wants data that is in-distribution (meaning within-capabilities) and tools that enables it to succeed. It probably hates wonky prompts and wonky tools. The LLM wants a platform to be able to do whatever it wants to solve said problem.
They all need a harness. Philosophically, the harness is the hub that connects all of this. It's the firelink shrine of agentic software.
In less fancy terminology, the harness is the Operating System for the LLM.

Quick Note on the "Pareto Frontier"

To optimize anything (including a harness), there are always trade-offs.
You often care about more than one objective at the same time. The Pareto frontier is the set of solutions where you cannot improve one objective without making another one worse.
In this paper, the two objectives they care about are:
  • Accuracy - how well the harness performs on the task
  • Token cost - how many context tokens the harness uses
The goal of the paper is to search for a harness that LIVES on the Pareto frontier. A harness lives on the Pareto frontier if there is no other harness that is both more accurate AND cheaper at the same time!
The goal of any kind of research (including these "agent-driven researches") is to constantly push that frontier forward.
But before we could optimize all that, we should probably be more definitive about what a harness actually is.

The Components of a Harness

A harness includes:
  1. Pre and Post Hooks: Transformations of the inputs that run before the prompt is sent to the model (pre-hook) and transformations of model or tool outputs (post-hook) before it is sent downstream
  2. Prompt building: The way the system prompt and user prompt is created based on current context clues. This could include things like the user's subscription tiers, active tools, and special instructions corresponding to operating modes (Claude Code's "plan" or "build" mode). This also includes lazy loading of prompts (aka SKILLS)
  3. Tools: What external tools the LLM can call. Websearch? Bash? Patch edits? Regex searches? Calculator? Phone a friend? The harness not only makes these definitions available in the LLM's context, but also it actually executes them on the LLM's behalf and return it the results.
  4. Memory: LLMs are transactional - they don't remember any past interaction beyond their current request. You have to round-trip past messages to keep their memory updated. Memory can be limited to current session (this conversation), or previous sessions (user's profile), or even organization level if engineered that way.
  5. External Data Sources: This basically comes either under pre-hooks and tools and/or memory. All kinds of "Retrieval Logic" belongs in the harness - from filesystem, websites, external databases, past messages, to hacking into somebody's whatsapp.


This is too complex, that's way too many variables to optimize!

Correct!
The cool thing about this paper is we won't be treating this as a component selection/optimization problem at all.
We will be treating this as a code optimization problem. Follow this chain on thought:
1. Every harness is code
2. That code defines everything that happens around the LLM call
3. The code lives in (say) a single Python file/repo
4. If we change the code, the harness changes
5. When harness changes, we can run an evaluation.
6. When we run the evalution we know it's accuracy and token cost.
7. We can then plot it on the Pareto Frontier
8. We can make more changes by learning from past mistakes
BOOM. That's an optimization loop!
Not quite.
The jump from point 7 to point 8 requires hours of experimentation and debugging!
Most of us writing evals are using one or two numeric metric to define how good a harness is. While this abstraction (accuracy and total tokens) is great for us to rate the quality of a harness, it is not enough to actually optimize!
Couple of numbers cannot tell the whole story.
We need:
  1. More than just metrics
  2. Delegate more work to AI agents and find more time to doom-scroll on Tiktok.
Let's discuss what the ACTUAL problem really is.

The Problem

People think that they the final form of AGI will come as a harness, not as a standalone LLM.
Meaning, the LLM + the Harness = the Product.
The way most harnesses are currently developed is very human-centric. Engineers spend weeks "vibes-checking" prompts and manually tweaking retrieval/tool/execution logic.
The paper argues that harnesses have become too complex for humans to optimize by hand.
This is a key technical insight from the paper - optimizers (like DSPy or prompt-tuning tools) often compress feedback too much.
  • We look at a single score (e.g., "Accuracy: 0.8") and try to change the harness based on that.
  • Meta-Harness argues that to build a good "OS," the optimizer needs rich, execution-level traces. It needs to see exactly where the bash command failed or why the memory retrieval fetched a useless chunk.
What if could improve our harnesses based on rich prompt feedbacks generated from our current harness?

The Meta-Harness

The Stanford paper propose Meta-Harness, an automated "outer-loop" optimization system that treats the development of LLM-based applications as a software engineering search problem.
Instead of a human engineer manually refining a system, Meta-Harness uses an "agentic proposer" to iteratively write, test, and improve the Python code that manages an underlying "base" model.

The Agentic Proposer

In the paper's experiments, the Agentic Proposer is Claude Code (powered by Claude 3.5 Sonnet/Opus), which is given a set of developer tools to interact with a filesystem.
Unlike other "prompt optimizers" that might just tweak some text, the proposer has the power to:
  • Rewrite logic: Change how the system retrieves data, how it manages memory, or how it constructs multi-step prompts.
  • Navigate history: Use tools like grep and cat to search through a history of its own previous attempts.
  • Reason causally: By looking at the execution traces (the exact inputs and outputs of a failed run), the agent can infer why a change didn't work and adjust its strategy accordingly.
The proposer (Claude Code) operates inside a Git-like repository that maintains a full history of the search. The filesystem structure is carefully designed to be searchable via standard terminal tools:

Filesystem-as-Feedback

Meta-Harness uses a filesystem as an external database to log all it's experiments.
It is a full history of prior experience (According to one of the main authors
@yoonholeee
himself, "this directory gets very big")
For every candidate the harness created, the system logs:
  1. The full source code of the harness.
  2. The performance scores (e.g., accuracy, token cost).
  3. The execution traces, including raw model prompts, tool calls, and state updates.
This allows the proposer to "read broadly across prior code and logs" to identify successful patterns and avoid repeating past mistakes.


The Optimization Loop

The authors find that unrestricted access to all previous history is essential, because the dependencies are so long-horizon.
Previous text optimization loops that only see rewards/summaries/previous attempts discard important information and underperform here.
The system follows a continuous cycle:
  1. Inspection: The proposer searches the filesystem for prior results and traces.
  2. Diagnosis: It reasons about failure modes (e.g., "The retrieval step is fetching irrelevant documents").
  3. Proposal: It writes a new version of the harness code (usually a single-file Python program)
  4. Evaluation: The system runs the new harness on a task distribution X and records the reward r(τ,x)
  5. Update: The results are added back to the filesystem, and the loop continues.

Search Objectives

Meta-Harness can optimize for multiple goals simultaneously (not just task-accuracy). If there's a trade-off between accuracy and context cost (the number of tokens used), the system identifies the Pareto frontier, i.e. the set of solutions that offer the best possible balance of both.

Case Studies They Did

They did a bunch, let's look at two!
1: Online Text Classification
The goal here was to manage a growing context of labeled examples efficiently. Meta-Harness was compared against two state-of-the-art context management systems, across three datasets: USPTO-50k (chemistry), Symptom2Disease (medical), and LawBench (legal)
The core discovery was about how you interrogate your memory. The system came up with a single, richly structured call that does three things:
  1. Label Primer: Lists all valid output labels upfront so the model sees the full answer space before any examples.
  2. Coverage Block: Retrieves one query-relevant example per label, ensuring every class is represented.
  3. Contrastive Block: Builds pairs of highly similar examples with different labels using TF-IDF, sharpening local decision boundaries around the current query.

Experiment 2: Terminal-Bench 2
We saw an experiment that was a "narrow" task. Now let's see a more general task. Terminal Bench.
What is Terminal Bench? TerminalBench-2 is a benchmark of 89 challenging tasks requiring long-horizon, fully autonomous execution. Things like setting up servers, assembling protein structures, running rendering pipelines, and solving cryptographic challenges.
Meta Harness does not make a harness from scratch. It starts from two baselines: the Terminus 2, and the Terminus-KIRA.
This iterative refinement that happens read like a story book, they have given a full descriptive breakdown of each step of the iterative process. The basic gist is that it tried and failed to beat the benchmark for multiple iterations and eventually tried a "one-shot environment snapshot" prompt that became the first candidate to beat the baseline.
Basically the original harness spent a few tool calls to get environmental descriptions of the system. Meta-Harness changed the code so that the initial LLM call itself already contains snapshots that the LLM regularly queries for, things like the working directory, a listing of /app (truncated to 20 entries for large directories), available programming languages and their versions, installed package managers (pip, apt-get), and available memory. This eliminates the 2–4 exploratory turns that agents typically spend discovering what tools and files are available, allowing the model to begin productive work immediately!
Without the Meta-Harness having explicit access to the logs and experiment traces, this optimization would simply not be possible at all, since the optimizer would never know how the internal tools operate.

Practical Implementation Tips (by the authors)


The coolest part of the paper was a "practical implementation tips" section. I won't go through all of them, but it is a short section with a few pointers that would benefit you greatly if you are developing harnesses yourself.
1. Write a Good Skill (Most Important Lever)
The skill text is the primary steering interface for the proposer. It should specify what is forbidden, what artifacts to produce, and what objective to optimize.
Run a few short debug runs (3–5 iterations) specifically to refine the skill before committing to a full run.

2. Start With a Baseline That Struggles
Write a simple baseline (e.g., few-shot prompting) first. Keep the search set small enough for roughly ~50 full evaluations per run - a fast, discriminative eval when you are prototyping the proposal agent.
3. Log Everything in a Navigable Format
Use machine-readable formats like JSON, structure the logs herirarchically.
4. Build a Small CLI Over the Logs This makes it easy for the optimizer to run fast queries to learn about the state of the experiment globally. CLI tool could :
  • List the Pareto frontier of best harnesses
  • Show top-k candidates
  • Diff code and results between pairs of runs

5. Warm-starts
Authors also point out that, If offline experience exists (other model rollouts, solved corpora), convert it into the same directory structure to warm-start exploration

6. Automate Evaluation Outside the Proposer
Running evals is too simple to delegate to the proposer. Use a separate harness that scores candidates and writes results to the filesystem

So... it's autoresearch for harnesses?

I think the ideas are very similar personally. My main takeaway is actually the simplicity of both the approaches. Recently Meta AI also published work on DGM-H (Darwin Godel Hyperagents) which I also wrote a paper review on (
https://x.com/neural_avb/status/2037526862964969583?s=20
) and I must say that this approach feels a lot simpler to execute.
The DGM family of research relies on recursive search, node-splitting, and optimizing any task from scratch by altering code. This system is much simpler and their tasks have been to improve existing systems.
While the architecture is simple, the computational space is not. Remember we keep the entire database of experiments in the filesystem and iterate on it (DGM discards solutions). So yeah, that stuff can get pretty token heavy. Maybe Claude Code isn't the best "harness" to use as the agentic proposer. Seeing Dr. Khattab and team also work on RLMs, I won't be surprised if they try to bind meta-harnesses and RLMs in holy matrimony later this year.
